summary: I read trajectory.py, world_mind.py, views.py and the tests end to end, then read every trajectory.md and journal.jsonl in artifacts/simulations_v4 plus all of artifacts/matched_pairs and artifacts/simulations_v3, tabulated all 32 runs' terminals, and computed for each one how much of its horizon it actually simulated before answering. The mechanical spine that was independently proved is genuinely sound and I confirm it: the compiler is frozen, replay is exact and non-vacuous from the on-disk ledger with zero model calls on all 31 completed runs, the resolution and shared_context never leave the roles allowed to see them, time never runs backwards, every event has a real cause, and no number decides how anybody behaves. But the system is neither mechanically correct at the terminal nor behaviourally believable: 3 of the 4 NO answers in the newest corpus were produced by advancing the clock across a horizon that was never simulated (0.0% of it lived) and are recorded as status 'cutoff' as though it had been; 44% of the committed record is device and channel bookkeeping; the event-quality review holds two rules that cannot both be satisfied for any act done through a device, so the decisive act of a scenario is deleted and its absence becomes the answer; and the same lease scene with byte-identical evidence answers YES in three runs and NO in three. The implementer's self-assessment is honest in its headline (INCOMPLETE) and unusually candid in most of its detail, but its section 19 heading 'the CRITICAL is fixed' is not supported by the corpus that section itself presents, and two of its evidence tables misreport the artifacts they cite.

findings.title: A final NO is still manufactured by a clock jump over time that was never simulated, and the artifact records it as an honestly reached horizon
findings.evidence: sworldmodel/semantic_runtime/trajectory.py:886-894 (empty-queue exit) and :807-816 + :827 (finish() with truncated=False advances the clock straight to the cutoff, judges final=True, and sets status='cutoff'). Measured over the corpus: artifacts/simulations_v4/case1_cold_email answers NO_AT_CUTOFF having committed 1 event and lived 0.0% of its 14-day horizon (last event 2026-07-27T14:00, cutoff 2026-08-10T14:00Z); artifacts/simulations_v4/b2_r1 (2 events) and b2_r2 (3 events) each answer NO having lived 0.0% of a 2d8h horizon. Only a2_r1 (100%) is an honestly lived NO. Same pattern in artifacts/matched_pairs/b1_okafor_herrera__r3 (1 event, 0.0%) and __r4 (0.0%). The test suite locks the behaviour in: tests/test_semantic_runtime.py::test_an_empty_queue_before_the_horizon_asks_everyone_before_giving_up asserts traj.status in ('cutoff','resolved','incomplete'), and ::test_reaching_the_horizon_is_recorded_so_the_run_stays_replayable asserts status=='cutoff' for a run in which nothing whatever happens.
findings.why_it_matters: NO_AT_CUTOFF is a claim about the absence of an event across a whole window; it is only sound if the window was lived. Code already knows the difference between a truncation and a horizon and refuses NO for truncations (trajectory.py:795-805), but applies that rule only to the step and call ceilings, not to the empty queue that produces almost every NO. A consumer reading terminal_result.json cannot distinguish 'four days passed and he never replied' from 'nobody was asked anything after the first minute'. The last-call sweep added this pass is a mitigation, not the fix its own finding text prescribes, and the test written for it states in its docstring that no scripted case fails without it.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat an empty queue before the cutoff as a truncation: report status='incomplete', forbid NO_AT_CUTOFF, and reserve status='cutoff' for runs whose clock reached the horizon through scheduled events.

findings.title: The event-quality review holds an unsatisfiable pair of rules, so the decisive act of a scenario is destroyed and its absence is reported as the answer
findings.evidence: world_mind.py:322-334 lists both 'a device or a channel acting on its own -- the printer printing, the scanner saving' and 'several stages at once' as REVISE, while WORLD_SYSTEM:31-35 requires the world to emit only the next immediate step. artifacts/simulations_v4/b2_r2/event_quality_reviews.jsonl: Margaret's intention to print/sign/scan/email is proposed six times and refused six times -- c8 'Printing is a device action' (atomic), c10 'combines multiple stages' (bundled), c21 'the printer beginning to print is a device acting on its own', c23 'bundles multiple stages', c31 'Printing is a device action ... it should be part of a larger person action like "Margaret prints the lease and takes the paper"', and then c33 rejects the world's compliance with c31 verbatim ('Margaret prints the lease PDF, takes the paper, signs it with a pen, scans ... and sends it to Jian Wei') as 'combines multiple distinct stages'. Same deadlock in b2_r1 (c12, c14). The two attempts are then destroyed by trajectory.py:327-336 and Margaret's follow-up turn is refused by the continuity reviewer for 'repeats an attempt already made at 10:00' (b2_r1 c18) and abandoned; she is never heard from again, and the run answers 'No event shows Margaret actually sent the signed lease'.
findings.why_it_matters: The exact failure this is is described verbatim in the code comment at trajectory.py:337-343 as a thing that was fixed ('a woman who meant to sign a document and send it back did nothing for two days'). It is not fixed; it recurs in the newest corpus with the same actor role, the same rejection wording and the same outcome. A gate that no legal answer can pass does not filter the record, it deletes the event the question is about, and the terminal then reports the deletion as a fact about a person. Neither the second independent reading nor the persisted trajectory.md can catch it, because two readers of one record cannot disagree about an absence and the overruled proposal does not appear in the trajectory at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the machinery limb of the review and stop admitting delivery hops as committed events at all, since availability is already a code-owned property of a journal item; keep only the two checks (invented facts, decision-in-someone's-mouth) that are demonstrably right.

findings.title: The terminal is not reproducible on identical evidence: the same scene answers YES or NO on which way a stochastic reviewer resolves the deadlock
findings.evidence: I verified myself that the actor-facing evidence in artifacts/simulations_v4/b1_r1 and b2_r1 is byte-identical after name substitution (initial_actor_states.json, both arms). v4: b1_r1 YES, b1_r2 YES, b2_r1 NO, b2_r2 NO. Across corpora the same b1 scene answers YES in 3 of 6 runs (matched_pairs/b1_okafor_herrera r1 YES, r2/r3/r4 NO; v4 b1_r1/b1_r2 YES). The mechanism is visible inside one run: artifacts/simulations_v4/b1_r1/event_quality_reviews.jsonl c12 REVISEs 'Aisha prints the lease document.' as 'a device acting on its own' and c16 PASSes the byte-identical string four calls later as 'A person is acting'. The b1 YES also carries the cost of the deadlock: e35 'Aisha prints the lease document' and e46 'Aisha signs the printed lease document' are already committed when e57 'Aisha prints the lease, signs it, scans it, and sends the signed copy' commits three minutes later, so the record has her print and sign the same document twice.
findings.why_it_matters: The deliverable of this system is one answer to one social question. On evidence that is not ambiguous -- a woman who has returned every document within a day, said she was ready to sign, has the equipment, and has two and a half days -- the system returns a coin flip, and the flip is not the world's uncertainty but a review verdict that is inconsistent with itself on the same string in the same run. This also makes every matched-pair conclusion, in either direction, unsupportable at the sample sizes used.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the deadlock in finding 2, then re-establish the pair-B and pair-A rates on the repaired loop before any claim about evidence sensitivity is made.

findings.title: The committed record is largely a systems trace, and explicit non-events are committed despite both prompts forbidding them by name
findings.evidence: My own count using evaluation/interface_mechanics.py over artifacts/simulations_v4: 47/107 (44%) of committed events are a device or channel acting or a restatement that nothing changed; artifacts/simulations_v4/case3_group is 39/70 (56%). The measure undercounts: e172 'The notification for Bea's message on Tomas's phone fades away', e846 'The notification on Kwame's phone fades after a few seconds as the screen times out', e1449 'Kwame's phone remains in his bag, screen off, with all accumulated notifications unread' are all classified NOT machinery. Near-identical events recur (e1363 and e1377, one minute apart, identical wording; e1160/e1164/e1172, three events for one DM notification landing on Bea's lock screen within two seconds). Explicit non-events pass the review that forbids them: v4/case3_group e88 'The message from Bea sits unread on Tomas's phone', e230 'The notification for Ines's message remains on Bea's phone screen, unseen', e457 'The messages ... remain unread on Tomas's phone'; and on the current post-v4 code, artifacts/simulations_v5/case1_cold_email e30 'The email remains in Mark Cuban's inbox, unread.' Events also carry clock times inside their descriptions (e457, e762, e955), which WORLD_SYSTEM:85-87 forbids and no code enforces.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader of case3_group's trajectory.md does not meet four housemates arranging a birthday dinner; they read a notification log. The governing rule says LLMs write social meaning, and the majority of what they wrote here is not social meaning. It is also not free: every notification hop is a step, and the step ceiling was reached with the question unanswered.
findings.suggested_fix: Make arrival and availability code-owned journal state that never becomes a committed event, so the record contains only what a person did.

findings.title: A person with an obvious stake does nothing at all across four simulated days and 250 steps
findings.evidence: artifacts/simulations_v4/case3_group: kwame receives 19 actor calls and has 37 wakes scheduled for him, and issues 0 intentions across the whole run; no committed event in the 70-event journal is authored by him. Every non-machinery event belongs to ines, bea or tomas. The same case in artifacts/simulations_v3/case3_group behaves the same way. The run then terminates UNRESOLVED because 'Tomas and Kwame have not observed any agreement'.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the check that distinguishes a live social world from a stub, and it fails on the one scenario built to test it. The completion report presents this exact case as 'the direct proof of the repair' for the inert-actor defect; the artifact shows the defect in a different form -- he is now woken and consulted, and still never does anything, which is worse evidence than never being asked because it consumes the budget while producing nothing.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat an actor consulted N times with zero intentions and zero authored events as a run-level defect surfaced in runtime_metrics.json, not as a silent outcome.

findings.title: The report's section 19 claim that the CRITICAL is fixed is not supported by the corpus that section presents, and contradicts section 18 of the same document
findings.evidence: SEMANTIC_RUNTIME_COMPLETION_REPORT.md:370 heading '## 19. After the reviewers: the CRITICAL is fixed' and :372-375 'Both it and the verifier clock rule are now repaired'. The nine runs listed at :394-407 as evidence include case1_cold_email (NO over 14 days, 0.0% of the horizon lived), b2_r1 and b2_r2 (NO, 0.0% lived) -- i.e. C1 recurring three times in the corpus offered as its repair. C1's own prescribed fix at :326-328 ('treat an empty queue before the cutoff as a truncation, so such a run reports incomplete and may not answer NO') was not applied. Two later reviewers re-raise it as CRITICAL against the current code (reviews/causal_realism.json, reviews/time_causality_terminal.json). Section 18 at :521-524 still says 'Half the corpus reaches its answer by running out of things to do rather than by reaching the horizon.'
findings.why_it_matters: This is the one place where the self-assessment overstates in a way that matters, and it overstates the single most consequential defect in the system. A section heading asserting a CRITICAL is closed, in a document whose stated purpose is to state the blockers plainly, is the claim a reader will carry away; the contradicting sentence is eleven sections later. It also breaks the standard the report sets for itself at :126 ('every regression test below was verified to fail without its fix') -- the test written for this fix states in its own docstring that no scripted case fails without it.
findings.suggested_fix: Retitle section 19 to say the mitigation was added and the CRITICAL remains open, and move it under 'NOT fixed'.

findings.title: Two of the report's evidence tables misreport the artifacts they cite, in the direction that flatters the system
findings.evidence: SEMANTIC_RUNTIME_COMPLETION_REPORT.md:405 lists 'case3_group | NO | 6 events | 4/4 | 30 wakes' for artifacts/simulations_v4/case3_group; the artifact's runtime_metrics.json says status incomplete, answer UNRESOLVED, 70 committed events, and grounded_wakes.jsonl has 233 wakes. The line at :408 '4 YES / 5 NO' should be 4 YES / 4 NO / 1 incomplete-UNRESOLVED. Separately, :205-207 claims of the v3 group case 'It is 22 events across all four of them, none of it machinery ... the direct proof of the repair'; artifacts/simulations_v3/case3_group/journal.jsonl has 94 events, of which 51 (54%) are machinery under the report's own corrected measure.
findings.why_it_matters: The aggregate machinery correction at :185-198 is honest and self-critical, and the report earns credit for it -- but the specific narrative claim built on the group case was never retracted, and it is the one place the document asserts a clean behavioural win. A per-run table that disagrees with the per-run artifact undermines the re-checkability the report offers as its guarantee.
findings.suggested_fix: Regenerate both tables mechanically from runtime_metrics.json and grounded_wakes.jsonl rather than by hand, and withdraw the 'none of it machinery' claim.

findings.title: Three of the five declared wake provenances are dead, and what an actor actually sees on a wake is still a content-free 'time has passed, reconsider'
findings.evidence: trajectory.py:154-158 declares five; only 'world_process' (:396) and 'actor_plan' (:537) are ever scheduled -- 639 and 448 across all 1,087 wakes in every corpus, and zero for 'observed_event', 'known_deadline' and 'action_completion'. views.py:39-40 and :67 render ELAPSED_TIME_REASON, 'time has passed and you are looking at your situation again', whenever a wake carries no observed trigger event. Live effect in artifacts/simulations_v4/case1_cold_email/trajectory.md:59-76: mark_cuban is woken five minutes after an email that never arrived as an event, is shown '(you have not observed anything yet)' and 'time has passed and you are looking at your situation again', and answers 'No new information or tasks have emerged'. The completion report's section 8 states automatic 'time passed, reconsider' wakes are deleted; they are deleted from the scheduler and still present in the prompt.
findings.why_it_matters: The code comment at trajectory.py:687-688 names 'a vocabulary member declared but never wired' as the source of three live defects, and three remain. 'known_deadline' in particular means nothing anywhere brings a person back because a deadline they know about is approaching -- which is the mechanism that would keep a run alive to its horizon and so make finding 1 unnecessary.
findings.suggested_fix: Wire known_deadline to the cutoff the bindings already carry, and either wire or delete observed_event and action_completion so the vocabulary matches what the scheduler can produce.
